summary: In Greek mythology, Amphius son of Merops of Percote co-leads the Trojan allies from Adrasteia, Apaesus, Pityeia, and Tereia with his brother Adrastus. Their father, a seer, forbade the war; the brothers went nonetheless and Diomedes slew them together. A second Amphius, son of Selagus from Paesus, is a distinct Trojan casualty.
etymology: Homer (Iliad 2.830) and Apollodorus (Epitome 3.35) both call Merops' son Amphius (Ἄμφιος).

sections.heading: Son of Merops
paragraphs: In the Catalogue of Ships Amphius and Adrastus, sons of Merops of Percote — the prophet who excelled all men — lead the contingents of Adrasteia, Apaesus, Pityeia, and steep Tereia. Merops would not suffer his sons to go to war, yet black fate drew them on.

In Iliad 11 Diomedes kills the chariot-team and both brothers when the Trojans have seized the best men of their host. Wikipedia's Amphius article also lists Amphius son of Selagus from Paesus, slain by Ajax — a separate defender.

sections.heading: Homonym care
paragraphs: The atlas id amphius-meropsid is Merops' son. Distinct from his brother adrastus-meropsid, from the Argive king adrastus, and from Amphius son of Selagus.
